entries.sentence: Shingles is a painful rash caused by the chickenpox virus becoming active again after lying dormant in the body.

entries.sentence: Shingles comes from the same virus that causes chickenpox, which stays dormant in the body and can reactivate later.
The NHS describes tingling or pain in an area of skin as an early sign, followed by a rash on one side of the body.

entries.sentence: The CDC adds that some people also have fatigue, fever or headache.

entries.sentence: In the UK, sudden severe symptoms or collapse are a 999 emergency.
The NHS describes the first signs as a tingling or painful feeling in an area of skin, sometimes with a headache or feeling generally unwell.
A rash then follows, usually on one side of the body.
The CDC says the rash is most often painful, itchy or tingly, and the NHS describes itchy blisters that later dry and scab.
entries.note: CDC painful, itchy or tingly; NHS blisters dry and scab

entries.sentence: Some people also have general symptoms of a viral infection, such as fatigue, fever or headache.
NHS Wales says the rash can sit in and around the eye and can affect sight or hearing.
entries.note: NHS Wales: eye; sight or hearing

entries.sentence: A clinician can usually diagnose shingles from the rash itself, according to the CDC.
A clinical review notes that unusual presentations can make the diagnosis challenging in some people.
entries.note: Review: variable presentation and atypical cases can make diagnosis challenging

entries.sentence: The CDC adds that diagnosis can be harder in children and younger adults, especially when the illness is mild.
entries.note: CDC: hard in children and younger adults if mild

entries.sentence: Shingles is caused by varicella-zoster virus, the virus behind chickenpox.
After chickenpox, the virus stays dormant in the body and can reactivate later.
entries.note: NHS: dormant, reactivate; CDC/MedlinePlus: dormant in nerve tissue

entries.sentence: The CDC says the risk of shingles rises sharply after 50 years of age, and that people with weakened immune systems also have a higher risk.
entries.note: CDC risk by age and immunity

entries.sentence: NHS Wales says a person cannot get shingles from someone who has shingles or chickenpox.
The NHS says shingles itself cannot be passed on, but a person who has never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine could catch chickenpox from someone with shingles.
The CDC says exposure is through direct contact with fluid from the blisters, and NHS Wales says a person is infectious to others only while the rash is weeping fluid.
entries.note: CDC direct contact with blister fluid; NHS Wales infectious while oozing (also on a GP surgery page)

entries.sentence: The NHS names pregnant women who have not had chickenpox, people with weakened immune systems and babies under 1 month old as groups to avoid contact with.
The CDC says there is no cure for shingles, but antiviral medicine can help.
Early treatment can reduce or prevent severe pain and help blisters dry faster, according to the CDC.
The NHS says mild cases may need no treatment, while antiviral tablets may be offered for a weakened immune system, moderate or severe pain, or a rash spreading beyond the chest, tummy and back.
These medicines usually need to be started within 3 days of the rash first appearing, and the NHS says pharmacists can supply the same antivirals as GPs.
Pain relief medicine can also help, the CDC says.
A clinical review lists topical treatments, anticonvulsants, antidepressants and, in severe cases, opioids among the options for pain during an outbreak.
The NHS says the rash can take up to 4 weeks to heal, and that pain can persist afterwards but usually improves over time.
NICE guidance on nerve pain says referral to a specialist pain service can be considered at any stage.
entries.note: CG173 via CKS: consider referral to specialist pain service at any stage

entries.sentence: CKS says clinical judgement guides management in people who are immunosuppressed.
The CDC says the most common complication is postherpetic neuralgia, a long-lasting nerve pain.
The NHS also lists infection of the rash, scarring, muscle weakness and eye problems.
The CDC adds hearing or vision loss and encephalitis.
The NHS says Ramsay Hunt syndrome, which affects the facial nerve, is a rare complication.
If the cornea is involved, the CDC says treatment to avert permanent scarring is important for preventing lasting vision loss.
The CDC advises urgent care for eye symptoms and immediate medical evaluation for neurological symptoms away from the area of the rash.

The NHS says an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is the route when shingles is suspected and the person is pregnant, has a rash on the eye or nose, has changes to vision, or has a severely weakened immune system.
For other suspected cases, a pharmacist or GP appointment is the usual route, because antivirals work best when started within about 3 days.
In the UK, sudden severe symptoms or collapse call for 999.
The CDC says vaccination lowers the chance of shingles and makes it milder if it still occurs.
The CDC recommends 2 doses of recombinant zoster vaccine, known as Shingrix, for adults aged 50 years and older.
It also recommends the vaccine for some younger adults with weakened immune systems.
UKHSA says the UK programme now uses only Shingrix, a two-dose vaccine, because the older Zostavax vaccine has been withdrawn.

The NHS says the vaccine is available to people who turned 65 on or after 1 September 2023, to unvaccinated people aged 70 to 79, and to people aged 50 and over with a severely weakened immune system.

entries.sentence: UKHSA says eligibility for the immunocompetent is phased in by age, and from 1 September 2025 extends to severely immunosuppressed adults aged 18 and over.
Eligibility can change over time, so the NHS page is the reference for current rules.
